title: US Civil Rights Movement 1954-1968
welcome_lead: From Brown v. Board to the assassination of Dr King, walk through the campaigns that transformed American citizenship.

final_note: You have followed the long road from Montgomery to Memphis. The unfinished business of civil rights endures.

concepts.def: Supreme Court ruling declaring racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional.
Year-long boycott of Montgomery's segregated buses sparked by Rosa Parks' arrest.
Civil rights organisation founded by Martin Luther King Jr. and others in 1957.
200,000-strong demonstration where Dr King delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech.
Federal law banning discrimination on the basis of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
Federal legislation outlawing discriminatory practices preventing African Americans from voting.

walkthroughs.body_html: Brown v. Board of Education overturned the 'separate but equal' doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896). Massive resistance in the South — including the Little Rock Crisis of 1957 — followed. Rosa Parks' arrest in Montgomery (1 December 1955) galvanised a year-long bus boycott led by the young Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.

Student sit-ins (Greensboro 1960), Freedom Rides (1961) and the Birmingham campaign (1963) exposed segregation's brutality to a national television audience. Bull Connor's use of dogs and fire hoses helped shift opinion. The March on Washington in August 1963 pressed for federal legislation.

The Selma to Montgomery marches of March 1965 led directly to the Voting Rights Act. Tensions over poverty, Vietnam and Northern de facto segregation followed. Riots in Watts (1965), Newark and Detroit (1967), the rise of Black Power and the assassination of Dr King in Memphis on 4 April 1968 closed a transformative era.
